In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah al-Insan (Man).

Allah the Exalted says: "Has there come upon man a period of time when he was not a thing [even] mentioned? Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixed [from a few fluids], We put him to trial, and We made him hearing and seeing."

The exegetes agree that "hal" (هَلْ, "has") here means "qad" (قَدْ, indeed), i.e., the interrogative is confirmatory, requiring the answer "yes."

The word "al-insan" (الإنسان) in "Has there come upon man (al-insan)" — it has been said that it refers to the first man, Adam (peace be upon him), upon whom there came a period of time when he was not a thing worth mentioning. And it has been said that it refers to mankind in general, the sons of Adam; in that case the meaning according to the first view is that Adam (peace be upon him) passed through a period of time, said to have been forty years.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas: he was clay, then dried clay (salsal), until the spirit was breathed into him.

According to the second view, the meaning is that there came upon man a period of time: forty days as a sperm-drop, then forty days as a clinging clot, then forty days as a lump of flesh. All of that is a thing, but he was not "mentioned," i.e., he was weak. Both interpretations are possible.

The second occurrence of "al-insan" in His saying, "Indeed, We created man (al-insan) from a sperm-drop mixed," the scholars agree that it is general, referring to the sons of Adam, since it is they who were created from a sperm-drop mixed, i.e., of mixed fluids. Al-Fakhr al-Razi (al-Fakhr al-Razi) preferred that the word "al-insan" in both places has one meaning, namely the general meaning, so that the style is consistent without a difference between the two words, since there is no distinguishing indicator.

Perhaps the context contains an indicator that supports what he said, namely that His saying, "We put him to trial" (نَبْتَلِيهِ), is definitively about the sons of Adam, because Adam (peace be upon him)'s affair ended with hearing and obeying: "Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance. Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful" (Al-Baqarah 2:37), and there remained no room for his being tested; rather, that applies to his descendants. And Allah knows best.

His saying, "Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixed," contains a statement of the origin of human creation, and he has stages of existence after the sperm-drop: a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then another creation, and all of that comes from nothing before it, as He said: "And I created you before, when you were nothing" (Maryam 19:9).

The Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him) had already explained this at the noble verse: "And I created you before, when you were nothing" (Maryam 19:9).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful﴾. Here, guidance (hidayah) carries the meaning of clarification (bayan), as in His saying: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

Al-sabil (the way) is the straight path. In it is an explanation of the division of mankind into two groups: one who is grateful, acknowledging Allah's blessing upon him and responding to it with gratitude, and one who is ungrateful and denies it.

His saying ﴿whether he be grateful﴾ points to Allah's favour upon the servant. Allah has mentioned two great blessings:

The first: bringing the human being into existence from non-existence, after he was "a thing not worth mentioning." This is a great blessing in which the servant has no acquisition (kasb).

The second: guidance through clarification and direction to the path of truth and happiness. This is the blessing of sending the Messengers and sending down the Books, and the servant has no acquisition in it either.

The scholars have said: there are three blessings in which the servant has no acquisition:

The first: his existence after non-existence.
The second: the blessing of faith.
The third: entry into Paradise.

They said: bringing into existence from non-existence is a bounty from Allah, the Exalted, as He said: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows female [offspring] upon whom He wills and bestows male [offspring] upon whom He wills, or He pairs them, males and females, and He renders whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing and Competent﴾ [ash-Shura: 49–50]. And whomever Allah renders barren will never bear children.

The second: the favour of faith, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56].

It has come in the hadith: "Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition), and then his parents make him a Jew or a Christian..." the hadith.

That a child is born to two Muslim parents is not something he has any acquisition in.

The third: the favour of entry into Paradise, as in the hadith: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy."

Allah has mentioned two blessings explicitly, namely the creation of man after non-existence and his guidance to the way. The third comes implicitly in the mention of the outcome: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ [al-Insan: 5], because the righteous are the grateful, as indicated by the division: ﴿whether he be grateful or ungrateful. Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing Fire. Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ [al-Insan: 3–5].

His saying ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way﴾ [al-Insan: 3] has already been stated to be guidance of clarification.

The Shaykh (may Allah's mercy be upon us and him) has already explained general guidance (al-hidayah al-'ammah) and specific guidance (al-hidayah al-khassah), and the combining of the two in more than one place. At the opening of this surah there is an explanation of the origin of man, his position regarding the sending of the Messengers and their guidance, and the outcomes of his deeds, whether gratitude or ingratitude.

The Sunnah has come with reciting this surah in the second rak'ah of the Friday dawn prayer, together with reciting Surat as-Sajdah in the first rak'ah.

Ibn Taymiyyah said: reciting both of them together on that day is due to the connection with the creation of Adam on Friday, so that a person may remember on this day, which is Friday, the origin of the creation of his father Adam and the origin of the creation of mankind in general, and remember his destiny and end, in order to see what he is upon of the call of the Messenger ﷺ, and whether he is grateful or ungrateful. End, summarized.

The sum of all this is that he holds that the wisdom in reciting the two surahs at Friday dawn is that Friday is the day of Adam, peace be upon him: on it he was created, on it the spirit was breathed into him, on it he was made to dwell in Paradise, on it he was sent down to the earth, on it his repentance was accepted, and on it the Hour will be established.

As it has been said: Friday is the day of Adam, and Monday is the day of Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: on it he was born, on it the revelation came to him, on it he arrived at Madinah during the Hijrah, and on it he passed away.

Since Friday is the day of the first human's creation and of all his events: creation from non-existence, favour upon him by dwelling in Paradise, his existence upon the earth, and the receiving of repentance from Allah, that is, the day of favour upon him both sensorily and in meaning, it was fitting that the Imam be reminded, through his recitation of the surah "as-Sajdah" at Friday dawn, of what it contains of the story of Adam's creation in His saying: ﴿He who perfected everything He created, and began the creation of man from clay﴾ ﴿then made his offspring from an extract of liquid, despised﴾ ﴿then proportioned him and breathed into him of His spirit﴾ [as-Sajdah: 7–9].

In it is also His saying: ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, but the word from Me has come into effect: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾ [as-Sajdah: 13], which instils fear into the hearts of the servants, since it is not known which of the two groups one is in, so it makes him more eager to do good and more fearful of evil.

Then He warned against forgetting the Day of Resurrection: ﴿So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting of this your Day﴾ [as-Sajdah: 14].

Thus in the first rak'ah, the Muslim returns to the origin of his existence and recalls the story of the first human.

Likewise, in the second rak'ah it comes with his own story from the beginning of his creation: ﴿from a drop of mingled fluid﴾, and reminds him of the guidance that was sent down to him, encourages him to be grateful for his blessings, and warns him against denying and disbelieving them.

It has also shown him his end in both respects: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers chains and shackles and a blazing Fire﴾ ﴿Indeed, the righteous will drink from a cup whose mixture is of camphor﴾ [al-Insan: 4–5].

So when that reaches his hearing on the day of his creation and the day of his resurrection, on which the Hour will be established, it is as though he looks at and witnesses the beginning of his existence and the end of his destiny; so he does not deny the resurrection. He knows the origin of his creation and does not fall short in an obligation, and he knows his end. This is in the utmost wisdom, as you see.

(p-382) Among what supports what he went to, may Allah have mercy on him, is the consideration of occasions (al-munasabat), as in many matters, such as His saying: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed as guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and criterion. So whoever sights the month among you, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. All months are equal in terms of time, but because the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an was in this month, Allah made it a place of fasting, and honoured the whole Ummah and indeed the whole world through it. Paradise is adorned in it, the rebellious devils are chained in it, and deeds are multiplied in it.

Likewise, the night of it in which the beginning occurred, Allah singled it out from the rest of the nights of the month: it is the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr), which Allah made better than a thousand months, and that is only because, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1], the whole surah.

* *

Issue.

People have greatly disputed the consideration of occasions in Islam and its neglect, and excess and deficiency have occurred in it, and as it has been said: "Both extremes of the matter are blameworthy."

Taking our starting point from the words of Ibn Taymiyyah, we present this brief note on this issue: that by reflecting on the Shari'ah and the events of Islam in general and in particular, that is, in the general case of nations and the specific case of this Ummah, we find occasions to be of two kinds: an occasion that is considered, to which the Shari'ah has given attention because it contains admonition and remembrance that renew with the renewal of days and generations, and that return to individuals and communities with provision drawn from them; and an occasion that is not considered, either because it is limited in itself or because individuals cannot keep pace with it.

From the first kind is Friday. Some of the characteristics of this day have been mentioned in Surat al-Jumu'ah. Ibn Taymiyyah's statement, and Islam has given it attention in encouraging the recitation mentioned at the Fajr prayer, and in encouraging its observance and honouring it with ghusl, perfume, and early going to it, as has been mentioned in Surat al-Jumu'ah.

But without exaggeration or excess: the prohibition has come against fasting its day alone, without being preceded by a fast before it or followed by a fast after it, just as it forbade singling out its night for standing in prayer. The texts on this are mutually reinforcing and established. So it is a considered occasion, with moderation and turning to Allah, that is, without excess or deficiency.

(p-383) From them is Monday, as we have already mentioned. It has come from him ﷺ that he was asked about fasting on Monday, and he said: "This is a day on which I was born, and on which it was revealed to me." It was the day of his arrival at Madinah in the Hijrah, and it was the day of his death ﷺ. He ﷺ honoured it because of the causes mentioned, all of which are great events and noble occasions.

On the day of his birth ﷺ there occurred cosmic signs, beginning with the event of Abrahah and the destruction of his army, as a prelude (irhas) to his birth ﷺ, then the appearance of a star "of the Khitan." It was reported that his mother, when she was pregnant with him, was told that she had conceived the master of this Ummah, and that when he came into the world she should say: "I seek refuge for him in the One from the evil of every envier," and then name him Muhammad. Ibn Hisham mentioned that when she was pregnant with him she saw a light come out of her by which she saw the palaces of Busra in the land of Sham.

Ibn Hisham also mentioned that Hassan ibn Thabit, while still a boy, heard a Jew shouting at the top of his voice from a fort in Yathrib: "O assembly of the Jews!" When they gathered to him they said: "Woe to you! What is the matter with you?" He said: "Tonight the star of Ahmad, in whom he was born, has risen."

Ibn Kathir in his history, al-Bayhaqi in his Dala'il, and Ibn Hisham in his Sirah related numerous reports of what the world witnessed on the night of his birth ﷺ; we summarize from them the following:

From Uthman ibn Abi al-As: that his mother attended his birth ﷺ, and she said: "I saw nothing in the house except light, and I was looking at the stars coming close until I said: they will surely fall upon me."

And from Abu al-Hakam al-Tanukhi, who said: when a child was born in Quraysh they would hand him over to women who would turn a cooking pot over him until morning. They turned a pot over him ﷺ, and it split apart, and he was found with his eyes open, fixing his gaze upon the sky.

His birth had cosmic events that caught the attention of the whole world.

Ibn Kathir mentioned among them: the idols overturned upon their faces, the palace of Kisra shook and some of its battlements fell, the fire of Persia went out, which had not been extinguished before, and the lake of Sawah dried up. In this there was a prelude (irhas) to the breaking of idols, the spread of Islam, and the entry of the Persians into Islam. Then the beginning of revelation (p-384) came to him ﷺ on a Monday.

* *

The celebration of this day.

There is no doubt that the world has not witnessed two events greater than these two events: the birth of the master of creation, and the beginning of the sending down of the best of Books. He ﷺ used to honour it, and that was by fasting, which is the prescribed act through which the Muslim expresses his feeling about it, and the pure worship by which he thanks Allah, the Exalted, for these two great blessings.

As for what some people do of celebrations and displays, that occurred after there had been none in the first century, nor the second, nor the third, which are the centuries attested to as good; its first innovation was in the fourth century.

People have divided over it into two groups: one group denies it and denies it upon those who do it, because the predecessors (salaf) did not do it, and no report has come about it. Another group considers it permissible, since there is no prohibition against it. Each group may press hard against the other on this issue.

Ibn Taymiyyah, in Iqtida' al-Sirat al-Mustaqim, has a moderate statement of the utmost fairness, of which we cite the essence for its eloquence, and Allah is the Guide to the right path.

Ibn Taymiyyah said, in a section he devoted to innovated festivals: he mentioned the first Friday of Rajab and the festival of Khumm on the eighteenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, when he ﷺ gave a sermon and urged following the Sunnah and his family (ahl al-bayt). Then he came to the practice of the Mawlid, and said:

And likewise is what some people innovate, either in imitation of the Christians regarding the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him, or out of love for the Prophet ﷺ and exalting him. Allah may reward them for this love and this striving, but not for the innovations of making the Prophet's ﷺ birthday (mawlid) a festival, especially as people differ about the date of his birth, whether it was in Rabi' or in Ramadan. The righteous predecessors (al-salaf), may Allah be pleased with them, did not do this, although the reason for it existed and there was no obstacle to it.

Had this been pure good or preponderant good, the predecessors, may Allah be pleased with them, would have been more entitled to it than us, for they had greater love for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and greater exaltation of him than we do, and they were more eager for good.

The perfection of love for him and exalting him lies only in following him, obeying him, adhering to his command, and reviving his sunnah (the prescribed way of the Prophet) inwardly (p-385) and outwardly, spreading what he was sent with, and striving for that with the heart, the hand, and the tongue. This is the path of the foremost early believers among the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar), and those who followed them in goodness. Yet most of those whom you see being greedy for such innovations, despite their good intention and striving for which they hope for reward, you find lukewarm about what the Messenger commanded them to be energetic about. They are like one who adorns the Mushaf but does not read it or follow it, and like one who decorates the mosque but does not pray in it, or prays in it only a little, and like one who acquires ornate lamps and carpets and similar outward adornments that were not prescribed, accompanied by showing off, pride, and preoccupation away from what is prescribed, which corrupts the state of their owner.

Know that among actions there are some in which there is good because they include types of what is prescribed, and in which there is also innovation and other things. Then he laid down the path of sound action for the individual in himself, and for the one calling others. He said: "So here you have two principles. The first: that your eagerness be to adhere to the sunnah, inwardly and outwardly. The second: that you call people to the sunnah according to your ability. So when you see someone doing this, and he will not abandon it except for something worse than it, do not call to abandoning a wrong by doing something more wrong than it, or by abandoning an obligatory or recommended act whose abandonment is more harmful than doing that disliked thing."

"But if there is some kind of good in the innovation, then replace it with prescribed good according to your ability, for souls do not give up one thing except for another. No one should abandon a good except for its like or for something better than it. For just as those who perform these innovations are blameworthy, having committed something disliked, those who abandon the sunan (recommended prescribed practices) are also blameworthy."

"Many of those who reject the innovations in acts of worship, you find them falling short in performing the sunan in these matters, or in commanding them. . . "

"Perhaps the state of many of them is worse than the state of one who performs those customs, which include some degree of disliked matters. Rather, religion is commanding the good and forbidding the wrong. So exalting the mawlid and taking it as a festive occasion may be done by some people, and they may have great reward in it for the goodness of their intention and their exaltation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, as I have already mentioned to you that some things are good from some people which are disliked from the committed believer who is upright."

(p-386) For this reason it was said to Ahmad: "Some of the rulers spend a thousand dinars and the like on a Mushaf." He said: "Leave him, for this is the best thing that gold can be spent on," or as he said, although his school holds that ornamenting the Mushafs is disliked. Such people, if they do not do this, will instead exchange it for corruption in which there is no good, such as spending it on books of immorality, like the books of tales and entertainment, or the wisdom of Persia and Rome.

The levels of actions are three. The first: a righteous action that is prescribed and in which there is no disliked element. The second: a righteous action that is good in some or most of its aspects, either because of a good intention or because it includes, along with that, types of what is prescribed. The third: what has no goodness in it at all.

As for the first, it is the sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it is the actions of the foremost early believers. As for the second, it is very numerous in the ways of later people who attribute themselves to knowledge or worship, and among the common folk too. These are better than those who do no righteous prescribed action and no unprescribed action. Yet the believer recognizes the good and denounces the wrong, and is not prevented from this by the agreement of some hypocrites with him in outward appearance regarding that good and the prohibition of that wrong, nor by the disagreement of some scholars of the believers. These matters and their like are what must be known and acted upon. Ends.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, treated this issue with the wisdom of the caller and the strategy of da'wah (calling to Islam), in a manner that leaves no room for dispute about it.

However, after him, may Allah have mercy on him, there have occurred matters that did not exist before, with which the Western world has been afflicted, and with which it has invaded the Eastern world, and with which the Muslims have been deceived. These are those destructive ideologies and the intellectual invasion, and the promotion of figures with economic or "salafi" (in the sense of doctrinaire) principles whose standing rose among their own people, and whose poisons were spread to our own kin. They began to set up commemorations for them and to present studies about them, out of ignorance or misguidance. Then some Muslims arose and said:

"We know that the mawlid is not a prophetic sunnah, nor a salafi path, nor a practice of the generations to which goodness is attested. We only want to confront an idea with an idea, and commemoration with commemoration, so as to gather the youth of the Muslims (p-387) around the biography of the Master of the Messengers, and this would be of the type: 'New rulings are introduced for people in proportion to the innovations they introduced,' and so on to the end."

Here one should not hasten to answer, but proceeding from the words of Ibn Taymiyyah quoted earlier, it may be said: If the aim is reviving the remembrance of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, then Allah the Exalted has already taken care of that in the broadest scope, for He joined the remembrance of His Messenger ﷺ with His own remembrance in the two testimonies (shahadatayn), with every adhan on every minaret of every mosque, in every iqamah for performing a prayer, and in every tashahhud in an obligatory or voluntary prayer, which exceeds thirty times, aloud and silently. Aloud, it fills the horizon; silently, it fills the heart and the senses.

Then comes the practical remembrance in every small and great matter: in eating with the right hand, because that is the sunnah; in dressing by starting with the right, because that is the sunnah; in lying down on the right side, because that is the sunnah; in spreading the greeting of peace, and in every movement and stillness of the servant, if he observes in them that they are the sunnah from the Prophet ﷺ. And if the aim is to express love, and love is the true mark of faith, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, none of you believes until I am dearer to him than his child, his wealth, and all people."

For the reality of love is obedience to the one you love, doing what he loves, and leaving what he does not approve of or does not love. From this it may be said: whatever accompanies the act of the mawlid of frivolity, play, and unlawful mixing, and actions in forms that have no basis, must be abandoned, and the expression of his love ﷺ must be purified of what he does not approve of ﷺ.

The Prophet ﷺ used to honor this day by fasting. And if the aim is to confront an idea with an idea, then the reality is that there is no relation between the two causes, and no reason to link the two sides, due to the distance between them, like the distance between truth and falsehood, or darkness and light.

Nevertheless, if it is unavoidable, there is no reason to restrict it to a specific time; rather, the whole year is for holding studies of the biography (sirah), and informing Muslims, the young among them, the common people, and others, about what you want of study of the prophetic biography.

In conclusion: instead of a negative stance of harsh denunciation, let it be a positive action containing wisdom and guidance toward what is better, according to what is possible, as Ibn Taymiyyah said. And success is from Allah the Exalted.

Among the occasions is the Night of Decree, for the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an in it, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. Then He explained its value by His saying: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 3], and He explained its distinctive features by His saying: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein by permission of their Lord, with every matter﴾ ﴿Peace it is until the emergence of dawn﴾ [al-Qadr: 4–5].

* *

Its honoring.

The Prophet ﷺ explained this by saying: "Seek it in the last ten nights, and in the odd nights of the last ten." He used to seclude himself (i'tikaf) for all ten nights, seeking that night. He would spend it standing in prayer in his seclusion, as came in the hadith: "When the last ten nights came, he would tighten his waist-wrap, spend the night awake, and wake his family." He did not play, nor joke, nor even sleep, but strove in worship.

Likewise the whole month of Ramadan, for the Qur'an was also sent down in it, as the reference to it has already passed. So its honoring is by fasting its days and standing in prayer during its nights, not by amusements, games, and parties. Its perfection has been reversed by some who prepare means of special entertainment, thereby reversing the intention and opposing what is prescribed.

Among the occasions is the Day of 'Ashura'. It had an ancient history, and the Arabs used to exalt it in the Jahiliyyah and would cover the Ka'bah with a cloth on it. "When the Prophet ﷺ came to Madinah, he found the Jews fasting it, so he said to them: 'Why do you fast it?' They said: 'A day on which Allah saved Moses from Pharaoh, so he fasted it in gratitude to Allah, and we fast it.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'We have more right to Moses than you,' so he fasted it and commanded the people to fast it." It is a great occasion: the salvation of Allah's Prophet Moses from Allah's enemy Pharaoh, the victory of truth over falsehood, the triumph of Allah's soldiers and the destruction of the soldiers of Satan.

This is truly an occasion that every Muslim should care about. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ said: "We have more right to Moses than you. We, the company of the Prophets, are sons of one father, and our religion is one."

Its fasting was obligatory until it was abrogated by the obligation of Ramadan. Thus, despite the greatness of this occasion in raising the word of Allah and supporting His Messenger, Moses's ﷺ rejoicing in it was by fasting it in gratitude to Allah.

Likewise the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did, and this is the sound path and the noble prophetic sunnah, not what some common people and ignorant folk innovate of appearances and events that have no basis. Then comes the general action and the multiple occasions (p-389) in the rites of Hajj, among them the running (al-harwalah) in the tawaf. It was in response to the plot of Quraysh, who intended treachery against the Muslims during the 'Umrat al-Qada'. So the Prophet ﷺ ordered them to show energy in the tawaf. That was when Satan came to Quraysh and said to them: "These Muslims with Muhammad ﷺ have come to you, and the fever of Yathrib has weakened them. If you attack them, you will uproot them." Gabriel informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so the situation was very grave and difficult, since the Muslims had no reinforcement, and there was no way to withdraw, and they had to complete the 'Umrah.

So the wise response was to turn Quraysh's own plan back upon the polytheists and come at them from the same door by which they had come. The Prophet ﷺ said to his companions: "Show them strength today from yourselves." So they ran in the tawaf and displayed strength and energy that amazed the polytheists, until they said: "By Allah, these are not humans; they are like jinn." Thus they frustrated the opportunity for them, and the Muslims were safe.

It was more like the situation of Moses with Pharaoh: Allah saved His Messenger ﷺ from the treachery of Quraysh. So this action became perpetuated and legislated in every tawaf of arrival until today, even though the cause has ended, since the Muslims ran with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the Farewell Pilgrimage two years after the conquest of Makkah.

The scholars said: this action remained as an imitation of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ first, and as a reminder of this situation and what the Muslims endured at the beginning of the da'wah.

As for the sa'y (walking between Safa and Marwah) and the running in it, they came for what they contain of renewing certainty in Allah, since Hajar was left behind, and she is among the great ones who relied upon Allah, and she who said to Ibrahim:

اذْهَبْ فَلَنْ يُضَيِّعَنا اللَّهُ. "Go, for Allah will not abandon us." She was left until she ran to the end of the count, as the scholars of *al-fara'id* (the science of inheritance shares) say, and that count is seven.

For every number after it is a repetition of what came before it, as they said of the number of the heavens and the earth, the pebbles of the stoning, and the days of the week. Etc.

This was so that she might exert her utmost effort, and her hopes of help from the earth would be cut off. Then she would turn to the heaven with the strength of certainty and the intensity of supplication, and would direct all of herself, her feeling, her heart and her body, to Allah. Then the greatest help would come to her, as a blessing for her and for the Muslims after her.

That was a practical lesson, whose living on has been its renewal.

Thus it is with the sacrifice (*nahr*) and the story of the ransom. It contained a lesson for the Ummah, for its individuals and its community, within a complete family (p-390): a father, a mother, and a son, each submitting their leadership to the command of Allah, to the utmost limit of sacrifice, when Ibrahim said to Isma'il what Allah related to us: ﴿O my son, I see in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so consider what you think﴾ [al-Saffat: 102].

It was a grave event. What opinion could a son have about slaughtering himself? But it was the preparation for the command of Allah. So the son's stance was no less magnificent than the father's:
﴿O my father, do what you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. This was not merely an offer and an acceptance. The time of execution came to the point of zero, as it is said.

Everything proceeded toward execution: ﴿So when they had both submitted and he had put him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103]. How wondrous is this stance, which every statement fails to portray, every pen falters to explain, and every tongue is too heavy to express. An old man in his great age holds a knife in one hand and throws his son and his offspring down with the other. How did his hand become strong enough to hold the knife, and his eyes strong enough to see it in his hand? How did his other hand obey him in throwing his son down upon his forehead?

It is the strength of faith and the way of commitment. Here is the son with his father, subject to his hand, enduring for the command of Allah and submitting to the decree of Allah: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient﴾ [al-Saffat: 102]. The situation now: a father with the knife in his hand, and a son laid upon his forehead. Nothing remained but the holding of breath for the moment of execution. But the mercy of Allah is vaster, and His relief from Him is nearer: ﴿And We called to him, "O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ [al-Saffat: 104–105].

So it was a great occasion, and its benefit is immense. Islam immortalized it in the *hady* (sacrificial offering) and the *dhahiyyah* (sacrifice).

As for the stoning of the pillars, and so on to the end, all of these are acts of worship, rituals, and drawing near to Allah the Exalted, in detachment and severance (from worldly things), and in continual remembrance of Allah the Exalted.

There are great events and mighty occasions that are no less important than those preceding them, but Islam did not establish any specific commemoration for them, as in the Treaty of Hudaybiyah.

This treaty was among the greatest occasions in Islam, for in it was the extraction of Quraysh's recognition of the Islamic entity, leaning toward the treaty, and the covenant documented between the two parties. Allah named it a victory, as He the Exalted said: ﴿So He knew what you did not know, and He made, before that, a near victory﴾ [al-Fath: 27].

(p-391) The surah of "al-Fath" (The Victory) was revealed upon his return (ﷺ) from the Treaty of Hudaybiyah.

Likewise, the Day of Badr was the Day of the Criterion (*al-Furqan*), on which Allah distinguished between truth and falsehood, and gave the Muslims victory over the polytheists despite their fewness and the polytheists' greatness in number.

Likewise, the Day of the Conquest of Makkah, the smashing of the idols, and the final decisive end of the state of polytheism in the Arab lands. Before that was the night of his (ﷺ) departure from Makkah and his descent into the cave, for in it was his (ﷺ) deliverance from the treachery of the polytheists. As "the Siddiq (Abu Bakr) said while they were on the road to the cave, when he would walk sometimes ahead of the Messenger (ﷺ) and sometimes behind him. The Prophet (ﷺ) asked him, and he said: 'I remember the ambush, so I walk ahead of you, and I remember the pursuit, so I walk behind you.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Would you want, if anything should happen, that it would happen to you, O Abu Bakr?' I said: 'Yes, by my father and my mother, O Messenger of Allah. If I perish, I perish alone, but if you are struck, O Messenger of Allah, the call (of Islam) will be struck with you.'"

Likewise, his (ﷺ) arrival at Madinah was the beginning of a new life and the building of the entity of a new Ummah. All of that did not lead Islam to make any special act of worship for all of it. People, in its time, are seized by the emotion of remembrance, drawn by the longing for the past, and the pages of history appear before them. So do they stand deaf and mute, or do they speak with a word of expression and gratitude to Allah? If there is anything of this kind, it is by no means correct that it be part of idle play, amusement, or what is wrong, or what does not please Allah or His Messenger.

If there is anything of this kind, it is correct only if it follows the method that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laid down for such occasions, of worship through fasting, charity, or *nusuk* (sacrificial rites). It cannot be said of it what is said of the *masalih mursalah* (unrestricted public interests), wherever they are.

The age of legislation was (over) and nothing was legislated concerning these matters. Is the matter regarding them like the matter regarding the *mawlid* (celebration of the Prophet's birth), and would they fall within the generality of His saying the Exalted: ﴿And remind, for the reminder benefits the believers﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 55], and within His saying the Exalted ﴿So take warning, O you with vision﴾ [al-Hashr: 2], as an opinion regarding the stories of those who came before?

And we too, after these centuries, do we narrate to our generations the most important events of Islam in order to extract admonition and lesson, or not?

This is what can be presented briefly on this question. And with Allah the Exalted is success.

Note.

Among what is considered related to this topic in general is what Ibn Kathir reported in his *Tafsir* when discussing (p-392) the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion, and completed My favor upon you, and have approved Islam as your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

He said there: Imam Ahmad said: Ja'far ibn 'Awn narrated to us, Abu al-'Umays narrated to us, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq ibn Shihab, who said: "A man from the Jews came to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and said: 'O Commander of the Believers, you recite a verse in your book. If it had been revealed to us, O assembly of Jews, we would have taken that day as a festival.' He said: 'And which verse?' He said: 'His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾.' 'Umar said: 'By Allah, I know the day on which it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the hour in which it was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): it was the evening of 'Arafah, on a Friday.'"

It was also narrated by al-Bukhari, from al-Hasan ibn al-Sabbah, from Ja'far ibn 'Awn with it. Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i also narrated it through several chains from Qays ibn Muslim with it. The wording of al-Bukhari, when interpreting this verse, through the chain of Sufyan al-Thawri, from Qays, from Tariq, is: "The Jews said to 'Umar: 'You recite a verse which, if it had been revealed about us, we would have taken as a festival.' 'Umar said: 'I know when it was revealed, and where it was revealed, and where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was when it was revealed: it was the Day of 'Arafah, and I, by Allah, was at 'Arafah.'"

He related from Ibn Jarir: Ka'b said: "If this verse had been revealed to any other nation than this Ummah, they would have looked at the day on which it was revealed to them and taken it as a festival in which they gather."

'Umar said: "Which verse, O Ka'b?" He said: "﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾."

'Umar answered him with what he had answered previously, and said: "On a Friday and on the Day of 'Arafah, and both of them, praise be to Allah, are a festival for us."

It is related from Ibn Jarir, from Ibn 'Abbas: he recited the verse, and a Jew said: "If this verse had been revealed to us, we would have taken its day as a festival." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It was revealed on a day of two festivals: a day of festival and a day of Friday."

The point of citing it is that 'Umar heard the Jew praising the day of its revelation, and he approved of the Jew's statement and did not object to it, but informed him of the fact, which is that the day of its revelation is itself a festival, without our having to take it as one.

Likewise Ibn 'Abbas approved the Jew's report, his expectation, and his suggestion, and did not object to him, just as 'Umar did not object. This suggests that if the day of its revelation had not been a festival, it would have been possible for it to be taken as one. But it coincided with a festival, or two festivals, so it is a honoring of the day by reason of what was revealed in it of the perfection of the religion (p-393) and the completion of the favor.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We created man from a sperm-drop mixture (*nutfah amshaj*)﴾ [al-Insan: 2]. *Amshaj* means mixtures, as He the Exalted said: ﴿from a gushing fluid﴾ ﴿emerging from between the spine and the ribs﴾ [al-Tariq: 6–7].

* *

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We guided him to the way, either grateful or ungrateful﴾.

He the Exalted made clear that He guided man to the way, and that after the guidance he is either grateful or ungrateful.

This guidance is the guidance of explanation and direction, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. Likewise, true guidance is by the creation of success (*tawfiq*), a grace from Allah upon whomever He wills, as was mentioned earlier at His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love, but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ [al-Qasas: 56].

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had previously explained the reconciliation of these two verses, and the meaning of general and specific guidance.

Allah's saying: ﴿Chains and shackles﴾

He, may He be exalted, has explained the nature of these chains by their length, in His saying: ﴿Into a chain whose length is seventy cubits﴾ [al-Haqqah: 32].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They drink from a cup﴾

The root يَشْرَبُ (yashrabu, "to drink") is transitive by itself, so one says يَشْرَبُ كَأْسًا ("he drinks a cup") without the particle "مِن" (min). The particle "مِن" is used for partitive (tab'id, "indicating a part") and for origin or starting point (ibtida', "indicating a starting point"). It has been said that here it is for ibtida', and that the verb is made to imply (mudammana) another verb, namely "they enjoy (yatanaʽʽamuna)" and "they quench their thirst (yartawna)", just as they said regarding: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6]. This is because the particle "ba'" (bi) is used to express intention (iradah), and there is no intention here; rather, they enjoy it.

What appears to be correct is that "مِن" is partitive in meaning, and that the drinking of the people of Paradise is by way of luxury and delight, which is the custom of the affluent and pampered, who drink part of the cup, not all of it.

This is indicated by the fact that they do not drink out of thirst, as in the saying of Allah, exalted is He, to Adam: ﴿Indeed, it is granted to you that you will not hunger therein or go naked, and that you will not thirst therein or be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118-119]. The transitivity of (p-394) "they are given to drink" (yusqawna) directly to the cup will come later: ﴿and they will be given to drink therein a cup﴾ [al-Insan: 17], and there will come His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾ [al-Insan: 21].

This is supported by their agreement on the implication (tadmin) in: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾, where it is clear here.

And there, the partitive meaning is evident.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They fulfil their vows﴾

The discussion of vows (nadhr) was already presented fully by the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And let them fulfil their vows﴾ [al-Hajj: 29], in Surat al-Hajj.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they give food, in spite of their love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾

Scholars have differed concerning the referent of the pronoun in ﴿in spite of their love for it﴾: does it refer to the food, or to Allah, exalted is He? That is, "they give food in spite of their love for food, due to its scarcity among them and their need for it," or "out of love for Allah, hoping for the reward of Allah"?

Ibn Kathir preferred the first meaning, which is the choice of Ibn Jarir, and he cited as evidence such verses as: ﴿And he gives wealth in spite of his love for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], and His saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from that which you love﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 92].

In truth, the first line of evidence contains what is in this verse, but the closer and clearer proof is His saying: ﴿And they prefer [others] over themselves, even though they themselves are in privation﴾ [al-Hashr: 9].

In the verse that follows in this surah there is an indication supporting that the pronoun refers to the food, as explained above, namely His saying after it: ﴿We feed you only for the countenance of Allah. We do not want from you reward or thanks﴾ [al-Insan: 9]. This is because it carries the meaning of love of Allah, which makes the first [mention] refer to the food and this one to Allah. Establishing a new meaning is preferable to emphasizing an existing one, so the context would be: "and they give food, despite their need for it, and for the countenance of Allah, exalted is He." And Allah knows best.

Issue:

In His saying: ﴿needy, orphan, and captive﴾, three categories are gathered:

The first and second are, for the most part, from among the Muslims. As for the third, the captive, the Muslims had no captives except from the disbelievers. And although the surah is Meccan, the lesson lies in the generality of the wording, as is well known.

Ibn Kathir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that it refers to the Persians among the polytheists, and he cited the story of the captives of Badr.

Ibn Jarir chose that the captives are the servants. What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that the captives here carry their literal meaning, because servants do not fall outside the two categories previously mentioned, the orphan and the needy, whereas these captives, after falling into captivity, have no power or means left to them. Thus nothing remains but kindness toward them.

This is among the excellences of Islam and the loftiness of its teachings. The whole world today is in need of knowing these lofty heavenly teachings, even toward its enemies. Some of this has already been mentioned in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you over religion and do not expel you from your homes—from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 8], and these captives, after capture, are not fighters.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And He will bestow upon them radiance and joy﴾

The meaning of His words, the Exalted, ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] has already been discussed. Here He combines for them radiance (nadrah) and joy (surur). What appears to me - and Allah the Exalted knows best - is that the radiance is due to what they see of the bounties, and the joy is due to what they attain from looking at the Noble Face of Allah, as has been mentioned: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22-23]. So the joy is a consequence of looking at the Noble Face of Allah. - And Allah the Exalted knows best -.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver and cups that are [like] glass.﴾ ﴿Glass [made] of silver, which they have determined in measure.﴾

In it is the explicit mention of vessels of silver in Paradise.

And [the verse] mentions dishes of gold and cups, and these are prohibited in this world, as is well known. And God, exalted is He, has made clear that those who circulate among them are: ﴿eternal youths. If you saw them, you would think them scattered pearls﴾ [al-Insan: 19].

And the Shaykh (may God's mercy be upon us and upon him) had already discussed, in surah al-Tur, at his saying: ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys [serving] them﴾ [al-Tur: 24] (p. 396), that qawarir is the plural of qarurah, and the Arabs use qarurah specifically for a vessel of glass. But the verse is explicit that they are qawarir of silver, which indicates the correctness of applying qarurah to other than glass vessels, such as silver, for example.

The author of Lisan al-Arab said: al-qarurah is that in which drink and other things settle; it was also said that it is only of glass specifically.

As for His saying: ﴿qawarir﴾ ﴿of silver vessels﴾, some people of knowledge said: its meaning is vessels of glass with the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass. Ibn Sidah said: this is the best [interpretation]. End.

Ibn Faris said in Mu'jam Maqayis al-Lughah, under the root q-r-r: the qaf and the ra' are two sound roots, one of which indicates coldness and the other indicates settling firmly. Among the settling-firmly meanings he mentioned: istaqarra and mustaqarr, as the author of Lisan al-Arab also mentioned much of that. Then he said: from the same root is al-qarr (with a dammah on the ra'): pouring water into a thing; one says qarrartu al-ma' (I poured the water); and al-qarr: pouring speech into the ear. He mentioned from it al-iqrar (acknowledgement), the opposite of denial, because the truth becomes settled by it.

Then he mentioned the question of establishing language by transmission (sama') or by analogy (qiyas), saying: these are sound analogies. So either we go beyond [the transmitted usage] and bear the speech [beyond what was heard], as it has reached us that one of them said: the qarurah was named for the settling of water and other things in it, but this is not our position. We have said that the speech of the Arabs is of two kinds: one part is analogical, which we have mentioned, and another part was established by imposition (wad').

The matter is among the investigations of the principles (usul) concerning words: are they established by imposition that cannot be extended by analogy, remaining as the Arabs imposed them, or are they imposed by analogy? The benefit of the disagreement is whether all intoxicants, for example, are included in the term khamr by imposition, and so are prohibited by the text: ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90] and the rest of the verse, or whether they are prohibited by analogy to khamr through the common cause of intoxication. Accordingly, if the language supports extension by analogy, then it is stronger in ruling, in that the ruling comes by the text and not by analogy through the common cause. Perhaps the verified position in this question is what the scholars of imposition (ulama' al-wad') said: that languages are partly tawqifi (divinely taught/fixed by revelation) and partly qiyasi (analogical).

As for His saying: ﴿they have determined it in measure﴾ [al-Insan: 16], it points to the excellence of craftsmanship in making things equal in measure and proportion.

(p-397) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will be given to drink therein a cup whose mixture is ginger﴾

Before it, He said, exalted is He: ﴿whose mixture is camphor﴾ [Al-Insan: 5]. It has been said that both are together, so it is (cool) like camphor and (pleasant) like ginger.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 21:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And their Lord will give them to drink a pure drink﴾.

This is a description of the drink of Paradise, and the "drink" here is wine (khamr). The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had already explained this concept earlier: that the wine of this world is not pure, because the conditions of Paradise have their own particular rulings. What supports this is what preceded in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And there will be circulated among them vessels of silver﴾ [al-Insan: 15], even though vessels of silver are forbidden in this world, due to the hadith: "Whoever drinks in vessels of gold or silver is only swallowing the fire of Hell into his belly," and yet the people of Paradise are given delight with them.

Likewise, they are given delight with the wine of Paradise, and all of its descriptions in Paradise are the opposite of its descriptions in this world, as has preceded: ﴿They will not be affected by it with headache, nor will they be intoxicated﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 19]. The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, clarified this at His statement, exalted is He, in surah "al-Waqi'ah."

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p. 428) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Insan

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾.

It is not contradicted by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [al-Kahf: 31], and so on.

The reconciliation is evident: they are two gardens whose vessels and all that is in them are of silver, and two other gardens whose vessels and all that is in them are of gold. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 23:

Allah's statement: ﴿Indeed, We have sent down to you the Qur'an progressively (tanzil)﴾

"Nazzalna" and "tanzilan": they indicate repetition (al-takrar), unlike "anzalna." Allah has already made clear that He sent down the Qur'an on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in Surah al-Qadr: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1]. Here the text affirms progressive revelation (al-tanzil).

Allah has also explained the manner of the progressive revelation in His statement: ﴿And [it is] a Qur'an which We have separated [in revelation] that you may recite it to the people over a prolonged period. And We have sent it down in stages﴾ [al-Isra': 106].

Allah has also explained the wisdom behind this gradual revelation ("ala muktin") in His statement: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not revealed to him all at once?" Thus [it is], that We may strengthen thereby your heart. And We have spaced it out distinctly﴾ [al-Furqan: 32]. The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, has already presented the explanation of this issue in Surah al-Furqan, referring there to an earlier explanation.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 26:

Allah's statement: ﴿So prostrate yourself to Him, and glorify Him through the long night.﴾

The explanation of the amount of night-standing (qiyam al-layl) required of the Prophet has already been given at the beginning of the surah "al-Muzzammil" in His statement, (p-398) ﴿O you who are wrapped up in your garments,﴾ ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night, except a little,﴾ ﴿half of it, or reduce it a little,﴾ ﴿or add to it,﴾ up to the verse [al-Muzzammil: 4].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We created them and strengthened their joints﴾

Al-asr (binding, tying firmly) means tying with strength. It is derived from al-asr, which is the hide of a camel while it is still fresh, namely al-qadd (a strip of rawhide). A captive (al-asir) was named asir because his shackle is bound tightly with fresh camel hide. Here it means strengthening through firmly binding the moving limbs of the human body at their joints with sinews, and it is a metonymy (kinayah) for perfection and strength in creation.

Allah, exalted is He, has explained this in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created man in the best of stature﴾ [al-Tin: 4], and His saying: ﴿He who perfected everything He created﴾ [al-Sajdah: 7].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 76, verse 29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever wills takes to his Lord a way﴾

Here "sabil" (way) is indefinite (munkar), but it is specified by His saying: ﴿to his Lord﴾, because the way to his Lord is the straight way.

As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you"﴾ [al-An'am: 151], and at the end He said: ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it﴾ [al-An'am: 153], and that is the straight path to which he (ﷺ) called.

As in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ ﴿the path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [al-Shura: 52-53]. It is the Noble Qur'an, as was previously mentioned by the Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, in His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6]. Allah has made clear that it is the whole Qur'an in His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿This is the Book about which there is no doubt, a guidance for those conscious of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 1-2], after His saying: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾. It is as if He said: the one who guides to the straight path alluded to in al-Fatihah is the Noble Qur'an: ﴿a guidance for those conscious of Allah﴾ ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2-3], up to the end of the "attributes." So the way here is known.

His saying before it: ﴿Indeed, this is a reminder﴾ [al-Insan: 29] suggests that the way is by means of remembrance of it and taking admonition from it.

His saying: ﴿So whoever wills takes to his Lord a way﴾ makes the taking of a way to Allah dependent upon the will of whoever wills (p-399). Its qualification is the linking of the servant's will to the will of Allah, exalted is He, in His saying: ﴿And you will not will unless Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30]. This is the issue of qadar (divine decree).

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and upon him, had already treated this topic thoroughly at His saying: ﴿Would you compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99] in Surah Yunus, and referred to Surah al-Nisa'. However, His saying, exalted is He, as a conclusion to the noble verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Nisa': 11] indicates that everything that occurs in this universe of conduct and deeds occurs with knowledge from Allah and wisdom.
